title: Swindon's attacking black hole that they must fix to solve goalscoring woes
excerpt: Swindon Town have had one of League Two’s worst attacks this season — and there is a clear reason why.
content:
Swindon Town have had one of League Two’s worst attacks this season — and there is a clear reason why.

Swindon were consistently free-scoring during Ian Holloway’s first 18 months in charge but have become goal-shy this season. They have scored only nine goals in ten matches, none away from home.

By almost any measure, Swindon have had one of League Two’s worst attacks. According to WhoScored, they rank 21st for xG, 22nd for shots and 23rd for shots on target.

Injuries have clearly played a part, with several key attackers missing, but they are not the only reason Swindon are creating fewer chances.

One major reason is that this team has been built differently. After Town’s late-season collapse cost them a play-off place, Holloway made them more defensively solid by turning them into a high-pressing side built around hard-working players.

That meant moving away from playmakers such as Darren Oldaker and Billy Bodin towards harrying midfielders such as Jack Thomson and Anthony Munda. Defensively, the change has worked: aside from two heavy defeats, Swindon have conceded no more than once in any game.

But the trade-off has been a team that lacks creativity through the middle.

Their inability to work the ball into goalscoring areas can be seen by the fact that they have scored just one goal across the three games where they have held the majority of possession. Across the two where they didn't score, Town had a combined 0.13 open-play xG. This is not a team that can break defences down consistently.

Swindon Town's key passes against Crewe Alexandra (Image: Opta Analyst)

Opta Analyst’s graph of key passes from Saturday’s defeat by Crewe Alexandra shows only one coming from a central area — Stephan Negru’s pass out to the wing. The first-half pass map against Rochdale tells a similar story, with Swindon creating little through the middle.

Swindon Town's first-half pass map against Rochdale (Image: Opta Analyst)

Opta Analyst’s zones of dominance show opponents controlling those central areas, traditionally the most dangerous parts of the pitch.

Swindon Town have not controlled key areas of the pitch (Image: Opta Analyst)

The midfield three of Munda, Thomson, and Ollie Clarke have proved to be very effective at winning the ball back in midfield, but none of them has the craft to carve out regular chances.

No Swindon midfielder ranks among League Two’s top 100 for final-third passes. Only Thomson and Aaron Drinan rank ahead of Negru for open-play chances created, while Clarke leads Town for chance-creating carries but ranks 100th in the division.

As a result, Swindon often funnel attacks wide and look for crosses. According to WhoScored, 37 per cent of their attacks come down either flank, compared with 26 per cent through the middle.

Despite their strong individual form, Town may need to change their usual midfield three to add more invention.

Danny Butterworth is capable of beating players on the dribble (Image: Andy Crook)

Things might be different if Ben Middlemas were fit, given his incisiveness in that position, or if Joseph Hungbo played regularly, as his dynamism would force defences to adapt.

With attacking options limited, an immediate change is difficult, with many of those not presently starting not fully fit, but there are players they could turn to. Joe Snowdon could add creativity, Danny Butterworth has the ability to carry the ball through midfield into dangerous areas, and Jaylan Pearman remains a long-range threat who can pick a pass.

But for now, with Swindon having a black hole in the final third, teams have tended to block off the middle and put bodies in position to defend crosses, as can be seen with Town having one of the worst crossing accuracies in the division, as teams know that is where the ball is coming from.

Pressing has been a useful weapon, but as Swindon’s confidence to press aggressively has waned, their routes to goal have narrowed. That makes them easier to defend and keeps the vicious cycle going.
